lessons.title: EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales: When Debt and Capital Structure Matter

children.text: P/E compares a share price with profit after interest. That makes it a mirror of a company's debt as much as its business. Two companies running identical plants can show very different P/Es simply because one borrowed and the other did not. In capital-heavy Indian sectors like cement, power, telecom, metals and hotels, where debt levels vary enormously between peers, that distortion can flip a comparison entirely. Enterprise value multiples solve the problem by comparing the price of the whole business with the profit the whole business generates.

body.text: Match the numerator to the denominator. Enterprise value belongs to lenders and shareholders together, so divide it by profit available to both, such as EBITDA or EBIT. Equity value belongs to shareholders, so divide it by profit after interest, such as PAT. Mixing the two produces a meaningless ratio.

children.text: Building Enterprise Value for a Multiple

body.latex: \text{EV} = \text{Market cap} + \text{Debt} + \text{Lease liabilities} + \text{Minority interest} + \text{Preference capital} - \text{Cash and liquid investments}
body.caption: The same items as the Chapter 3 bridge, used in the opposite direction

children.text: The rule from Chapter 3 still applies: every claim you add to EV must have its share of profit included in the denominator, and every asset you subtract must have its income excluded. If you subtract cash, exclude interest on that cash from EBITDA. If you add minority interest, use consolidated EBITDA that includes 100% of subsidiaries.

body.title: Which multiple pairs with which profit

columns.label: Enterprise value multiples
points: EV / capacity, such as EV per tonne for cement

columns.label: Equity value multiples
points: Price / free cash flow to equity

children.text: Why Debt Distorts P/E: Two Identical Cement Companies

Two fictional cement companies have identical plants, identical volumes and identical costs. Each earns EBITDA of ₹1,300 crore, has depreciation of ₹300 crore and EBIT of ₹1,000 crore. The market values each business, debt and equity together, at the same enterprise value of ₹9,100 crore. The only difference is funding. Leveraged Cement borrowed ₹3,000 crore at 9%. Unlevered Cement has no debt and ₹500 crore of cash earning 7%.

body.caption: Same business, different capital structure (₹ crore, tax at 25%, illustrative)

children.text: On P/E, Leveraged Cement looks cheaper, at 11.1× against 12.4×. On EV/EBITDA, both are 7.0×, which is correct: the businesses are identical. Leveraged Cement's lower P/E is not a bargain. It is the market charging shareholders for the extra risk of ₹3,000 crore of debt ahead of them.

body.text: This does not mean EV/EBITDA ignores debt. It means it values the business first, before deciding how the value is split between lenders and shareholders. Leverage still matters to shareholders, and you deal with it in the bridge from EV to equity value, not by letting it distort the comparison of businesses.

children.text: Worked Example: A Cement Peer Set
Now four fictional listed cement companies with different balance sheets. Rank them first by P/E, then by EV/EBITDA.

body.title: The same four companies on P/E and EV/EBITDA

children.text: Peer B looks cheapest on P/E because heavy debt shrinks its market cap more than its earnings, but on EV/EBITDA it is 7.3×, not the cheapest business in the group. Peer C, carrying net cash, looks expensive on P/E at 14.2×, yet its business is the cheapest of the four on EV/EBITDA. The P/E ranking is Peer B, Peer D, Peer A, Peer C. The EV/EBITDA ranking is Peer C, Peer B, Peer D, Peer A. Comparing businesses in a sector where debt varies this much, EV/EBITDA is the more reliable guide.

body.label: Sector-specific EV multiples
body.context: Cement acquisitions in India are often discussed in EV per tonne of installed capacity. It is useful for comparing deal prices, but it ignores whether that capacity is efficient, well located or fully used. Pair it with EV/EBITDA.

children.text: The Ind AS 116 Trap
Since Ind AS 116 took effect for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2019, most lease rentals no longer appear as an operating expense. They are split into depreciation on a
right-of-use asset
and interest on a lease liability, both below EBITDA. Reported EBITDA rises, even though no rupee of cash has changed.

markDefs.definition: An asset recognised on the balance sheet under Ind AS 116 representing a company's right to use a leased asset, such as a store, warehouse or aircraft, over the lease term.

cells: When all peers report under Ind AS 116 and you add lease liabilities for each
EBITDA after deducting lease rentals paid
Comparing with older history, or with peers that own rather than lease their assets

body.text: The most common error is mixing the two: using reported, post-Ind AS 116 EBITDA without adding lease liabilities to EV. For lease-heavy businesses such as retail chains, quick-service restaurants, multiplexes, hospitals and airlines, this makes EV/EBITDA look artificially low. Many Indian companies in these sectors also disclose "pre-Ind AS 116 EBITDA" in their investor presentations. Use it.

children.text: What EBITDA Hides

EBITDA is popular because it is simple and unaffected by depreciation policy and debt. But it is not cash. It ignores the capital expenditure needed to maintain and grow the business, changes in working capital and taxes.

body.caption: Two companies at 10× EV/EBITDA with very different capex needs (₹ crore, illustrative)

children.text: Both trade at 10× EBITDA. After capex, the IT services company is priced at 11.1× and the telecom tower company at 25.0×. For capital-intensive businesses, EV/EBIT or EV/(EBITDA - capex) is a better cross-check, because depreciation or actual capex stands in for the real cost of staying in business.

body.caption: Justified EV/EBITDA: tax, depreciation intensity, growth, returns on new capital and WACC all matter

children.text: The justified multiple falls when depreciation is a larger share of EBITDA, when taxes are higher, when reinvestment is heavy or returns on it are low, and when WACC rises. A "sector average" EV/EBITDA hides all of these differences.
EV/Sales: For When There Is No Profit to Measure

EV/Sales is the multiple of last resort and first use. Last resort because it ignores profitability entirely. First use because, for loss-making companies such as many new-age technology listings, it is often the only multiple that exists. The key is to remember what it silently assumes about margins.

body.caption: An EV/Sales multiple is only as meaningful as the margin it implies

children.text: For a mature business with WACC of 11.5%, perpetual growth of 5% and a 13% return on new capital, fair EV is about 9.5× NOPAT. Now see what EV/Sales that supports at different margins.

A mature business with a 10% EBIT margin deserves only about 0.7× sales, and even a 20% margin supports only about 1.4×. So a loss-making company trading at 8× sales cannot be justified by margins alone. Suppose it reaches a 20% EBIT margin and a steady state in 10 years, and ignore any cash it generates before then. For today's price to make sense, revenue in year 10 must be about 16.7 times today's, growth of roughly 33% a year for a decade. That is the reverse DCF logic from Chapter 3, applied to a multiple. Chapter 5 values such companies properly.

body.text: Comparing EV/Sales across businesses with different margin potential is meaningless. A grocery retailer, a software company and a quick-commerce platform can all have revenue of ₹10,000 crore and completely different values. Only compare EV/Sales between companies expected to reach similar margins.

children.text: Choosing the Right Multiple

body.caption: A practical guide for Indian sectors

cells: EV/EBITDA, with EV/EBIT as a cross-check
Debt and depreciation vary widely between peers
EV/EBITDA on a consistent lease basis
FMCG, IT services, pharma with little debt
P/E, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check

No earnings or EBITDA to measure

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Calculate EV/EBITDA
body.prompt: A hotel company has a market capitalisation of ₹8,000 crore, borrowings of ₹2,500 crore, lease liabilities of ₹300 crore, minority interest of ₹200 crore and cash of ₹1,000 crore. Its EBITDA, reported under Ind AS 116, is ₹1,250 crore. What is its EV/EBITDA?
body.explanation: EV = ₹8,000 + ₹2,500 + ₹300 + ₹200 - ₹1,000 = ₹10,000 crore. EV/EBITDA = ₹10,000 ÷ ₹1,250 = 8.0×. Lease liabilities are included because reported EBITDA is before lease rentals.

body.title: Adjust for capex
body.prompt: A power generation company has an EV of ₹12,000 crore, EBITDA of ₹1,500 crore and annual capex of ₹900 crore. What is its EV/(EBITDA - capex)?

body.title: The low P/E steel company
body.question: A steel company trades at 6× P/E while its main peer trades at 11×. The first company has net debt of 3× EBITDA; the peer has almost no debt. On EV/EBITDA, both trade at 5.5×. What is the best conclusion?
options: The first company is almost half the price of its peer
The businesses are valued similarly; the first company's lower P/E reflects its higher debt and the extra risk to shareholders
EV/EBITDA is wrong because it ignores debt
The peer is overvalued because its P/E is higher
body.explanation: EV/EBITDA shows the market values both businesses at about the same multiple. The difference in P/E comes from capital structure: heavy debt shrinks market cap and earnings after interest, and shareholders demand compensation for the added risk. It is not a sign that the business is cheap.

body.title: The key advantage
body.textWithBlank: EV/EBITDA is useful for comparing peers because it is largely unaffected by differences in capital ___.
body.explanation: EV includes debt and EBITDA is before interest, so the multiple compares businesses regardless of how they are funded.

body.title: The cheap retail chain
body.scenario: Aarav, an investor in Lucknow, screens listed apparel retailers on EV/EBITDA. One chain, which leases all of its 600 stores, trades at 11× EV/EBITDA, while a rival that owns most of its stores trades at 18×. Aarav calculated EV as market cap plus borrowings minus cash, and used reported EBITDA for both. The first chain's investor presentation also shows "pre-Ind AS 116 EBITDA" that is about 40% lower than reported EBITDA.
body.prompt: Is the leasing chain really cheaper? How should Aarav redo the comparison?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The comparison is inconsistent. Reported EBITDA for the leasing chain is before lease rentals, because Ind AS 116 moved them to depreciation and interest. But Aarav did not add lease liabilities to its EV. The numerator excludes a debt-like claim while the denominator includes the profit that pays for it, so the multiple is too low.
2. The owning rival is not affected in the same way, because it has few leases. The two multiples are therefore measured on different bases.
3. Option 1: add each company's lease liabilities to EV and keep reported EBITDA. The leasing chain's EV rises and its multiple moves up.
4. Option 2: use pre-Ind AS 116 EBITDA, after lease rentals, and exclude lease liabilities from EV. With EBITDA about 40% lower and EV unchanged, the leasing chain's EV/EBITDA rises to roughly 11 ÷ 0.60, about 18×, the same as the rival.
5. Conclusion: on a consistent basis, the "cheap" retailer is priced about the same as its rival. Aarav should also compare EV/EBIT or EV/(EBITDA - capex), since store fit-outs and inventory differ, and check same-store growth before calling either one cheap.

points: Pair enterprise value with profit before interest, and equity value with profit after interest.
EV = market cap + debt + lease liabilities + minority interest + preference capital - cash and liquid investments.
Debt distorts P/E: identical businesses can have very different P/Es but the same EV/EBITDA.
Treat leases consistently: reported EBITDA with lease liabilities in EV, or pre-Ind AS 116 EBITDA without them.
EBITDA ignores capex, working capital and tax. Cross-check capital-intensive companies with EV/EBIT or EV/(EBITDA - capex).
EV/Sales is for companies without profits, and is only comparable between businesses with similar margin potential.
